One commenter refuses to install Node or use anything npm because of supply-chain compromises like the axios incident, saying other languages are better.

The malicious axios versions injected a fake dependency whose only purpose was to run a postinstall script that deployed a RAT. A commenter called this good news for pnpm/bun users, who have to manually approve postinstall scripts, unlike npm.

Workaround: npm now supports a minimum release age. Put `min-release-age=7` (days) and `ignore-scripts=true` in ~/.npmrc. Per the analysis, ignore-scripts alone would have mitigated the axios attack. The commenter found it 'wild' that npm, bun, and pnpm each use different time units for this setting, and warned that it makes LLM agents spin on install failures.

pnpm and bun now ignore postinstall scripts by default, but npm still runs them 'for legacy reasons.' The commenter recommends setting ignore-scripts=true in ~/.npmrc, since such scripts are mostly unnecessary.

Workaround: on Linux, alias npm and other package managers through bwrap with minimal permissions (no dbus or sockets, SSH via a forwarded socket). This limits the blast radius of malicious install scripts to the CWD and package caches.

A commenter asked for a mandatory 2FA step on publishing rather than fully automated releases. The compromised axios versions were published with stolen npm credentials, bypassing the project's GitHub Actions CI/CD.

Suggestion: since scanners catch these packages quickly, npm or a third party should offer a registry that only lets through packages passing scanners. Switching registries is just an `npm config set`, so a policy-gated registry is feasible.
"NPM gets worse than russian roulette. Perhaps we have to rename russian roulette to node roulette." Another commenter noted that running almost anything via npx would trigger the compromise.
"Sorry, but npm burned me too many times. It is (was?) the worst package manager I've ever used. Not a fan of npm the company either. I'm sticking with yarn."
"Thank god. NPM is so crappy it desperately needs institutional support."

A commenter reminded frontend developers that Verdaccio exists as a self-hosted npm registry alternative that is 'easy to implement, and relatively low maintenance,' in case GitHub/Microsoft ownership goes badly.

npm's ownership model is 'markedly less clear' than GitHub's registry, where packages must be scoped to the owning user/org. It has led to problems including package publishing rights being transferred to bad actors without anyone being aware.
The GitHub acquisition was seen as a good outcome: npm was a critical pillar of the software supply chain with an unviable business model, largely VC-funded.

A Python developer said the flood of tiny packages shows how well npm made publishing easy, so easy that people package trivial functions. By contrast, he would never publish a small package because of the overhead of setting up a pip package.
Several commenters said micro-modules weren't the real problem in the left-pad incident. The fault is in npm itself, because it is mutable and allows authors to delete published packages.
The real issue is the security hole npm opens up when a package name can be grabbed by anyone after the original developer pulls out.

Per npm download stats, 2,538,464 of left-pad's 2,550,569 monthly downloads came via the line-numbers package. That suggests few people depended on it directly, which highlights the need to vet transitive dependencies.
Workaround: instead of pulling tiny modules from npm, keep your own small modules inside the project and add them to package.json so they can be required anywhere.
"I absolutely loathe npm ci when checking out another branch. It is slow." The commenter asked how bun or other package managers compare.
